cards.text: Paul is writing to the church of God in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:1). He just told them, “I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you.” (2 Corinthians 7:16). Now he turns to something new: “Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia.”

The churches in Macedonia have been through a terrible ordeal and deep poverty, and they STILL have abundant joy. Friend, my edges went a little soft and I gave up and went quiet in the back of a drawer. These folks? Their joy is OVERFLOWING.

cards.question: The Macedonians are in deep poverty but full of joy. What does Paul say their joy and their poverty overflowed into?
Paul testifies about how the Macedonians gave. True or false: they gave only what they could afford and not a cent more.

cards.text: Nobody twisted their arm. Of their own accord, they come to Paul and earnestly plead with him. Friend, the only thing I ever pleaded that hard for was five more minutes on the oven timer.

cards.question: The Macedonians plead with Paul for the ___ of sharing in this service to the saints.
Paul says the Macedonians did even more than he expected. Before they gave themselves to Paul and his team, who did they give themselves to first?

cards.text: Now Paul turns to the Corinthians' own giving. Titus, Paul's partner and fellow worker (2 Corinthians 8:23), had already started their act of grace.

cards.question: Titus already started the Corinthians' act of grace. What does Paul urge Titus to do next?

cards.text: Then Paul brags on the Corinthians: faith, speech, knowledge, complete earnestness, and the love he inspired in them. They excel in EVERYTHING, and friend, the best line on my résumé is “presses dough, mostly straight.”

cards.question: Since the Corinthians already excel in so much, Paul tells them to see that they also excel in this grace of ___.
True or false: Paul says he is giving the Corinthians a command to give.
Paul isn't commanding the Corinthians. Instead, he's testing something through the earnestness of others. What is he testing?

cards.text: Then Paul points the Corinthians to the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Though He was rich, yet for their sake He became poor.

cards.question: Jesus was rich, yet for the Corinthians' sake He became poor. Why, according to Paul?

answers.text: So through His poverty they might become rich
So He could show the Macedonians how to give
So no one would ever envy His riches

cards.text: Paul gives his opinion: last year the Corinthians were first, not only to give, but even to want to. That's me with a new cookie recipe, friend: FIRED UP on Monday, and by Friday the dough is still sitting there… waiting… judging me.

cards.question: The Corinthians were eager to give last year. What does Paul tell them to do now?
Paul tells the Corinthians to finish according to their means. True or false: if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not what he does not have.
Paul doesn't intend for others to be relieved while the Corinthians are burdened. He wants there to be ___.
Right now, the Corinthians' surplus will meet the others' need. What does Paul say will happen in turn?

answers.text: Their surplus will meet Corinth's need
Corinth will be paid back double

cards.text: To wrap it up, Paul quotes Scripture. It's from when Israel gathered manna in the wilderness, and some gathered more, and some less (Exodus 16:17-18).

cards.question: In the Scripture Paul quotes about gathering, what happened to the one who gathered little?

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: 'The churches in Macedonia...', 'Friend, my edges went...', 'These folks?' and 'Their joy is OVERFLOWING.' It is not the opening card, so the limit is 2.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Nobody twisted their arm.', 'Of their own accord, they come to Paul...' and 'Friend, the only thing I ever pleaded...'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer 'The Lord' is two words. The wrong answers 'The elders in Jerusalem' and 'The church in Antioch' are four words each. The short right answer stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Card 8 says 'Now Paul turns to the Corinthians' own giving.' This gives away the answer to card 11, where the blank 'excel in this grace of ___' is answered by 'giving'.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The card only states facts. It has none of Papa Dorin's voice: no reaction, no comparison and no humor.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'The size of their savings' sounds modern and a little flippant next to 'The sincerity of their love' and 'Their loyalty to Titus'. It doesn't match their tone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The joke compares the Corinthians to a recipe started with excitement and left unfinished. That tells the baker the Corinthians stalled before finishing, which is the point of 8:11 and the answer to card 4 ('Finish the work'). It also rules out the wrong answer 'Start over from scratch'.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card only explains where Paul's quote comes from. It has none of Papa Dorin's voice. Stop 2 has one card with any personality (card 3).

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has 4 multiple choice cards, 1 true or false card and 1 fill in the blank card. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
